language_wrapper: Consider a wrap-around (torus) grid with {rows} rows and {cols} columns. We mark {num_centers} special cells at positions {centers_repr}. Every cell (i, j) is filled with the value equal to the negative of the maximum wrap-around Chebyshev distance from (i, j) to any marked cell, where wrap-around Chebyshev distance is defined by d_inf((i, j), (p, q)) = max(min(|i - p|, {rows} - |i - p|), min(|j - q|, {cols} - |j - q|)). A rectangular subgrid is formed by choosing a cyclic interval of rows and a cyclic interval of columns (each interval may wrap around). With radius r = {radius}, a subgrid S is called r-outstanding if every value in S strictly exceeds every value in any cell not in S whose wrap-around Chebyshev distance to S is at most r. The whole grid counts as an r-outstanding subgrid. Determine the number of r-outstanding (wrap-around) rectangular subgrids.
teacher_generator_code:
def generator(rng):
    # Choose grid sizes moderately small to allow strict brute-force verification, but nontrivial.
    rows = rng.randint(7, 12)
    cols = rng.randint(7, 12)
    # Pick number of centers between 2 and 4.
    num_centers = rng.randint(2, 4)
    # Sample distinct centers uniformly.
    all_cells = [(r, c) for r in range(1, rows+1) for c in range(1, cols+1)]
    centers = rng.sample(all_cells, num_centers)
    # Radius chosen to be the maximal possible torus Chebyshev distance so the ring covers all of the complement.
    radius = max(rows // 2, cols // 2)
    # Human-readable representation.
    centers_repr = ", ".join(f"({r}, {c})" for (r, c) in centers)
    return {
        'rows': rows,
        'cols': cols,
        'num_centers': num_centers,
        'radius': radius,
        'centers_repr': centers_repr,
        # hidden fields for verifier
        'centers': centers
    }

source_question: Let \(G\) be a \(499\times3997\) grid table, and a number is filled in each cell of \(G\). A rectangular sub-grid table \(S\) of \(G\) is called "outstanding" if the number in each cell of \(S\) is greater than the number in each cell outside \(S\) that shares a common vertex with \(S\). The grid table \(G\) itself is also an outstanding sub-grid table. Find the maximum value of the number of outstanding sub-grid tables.
